query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Minor Al addition induces coherent γ′ nanoprecipitates in a Ti–Ni primary HEA, thereby improving elevated-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: A cast high-entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as primary constituents, e.g. a Ti35Ni35Fe10Co10Cr10 (at%) composition exhibiting a single-phase matrix predominantly strengthened by solid solution effects.
generation.intervention: Replace 5 at.% of a minor element (reduce Cr from 10% to 5%) and add 5 at.% Al to yield a composition of Ti35Ni35Fe10Co10Cr5Al5.
generation.conditions: After casting, apply a homogenization heat treatment at approximately 800°C for 1 hour to allow controlled nucleation and growth of the precipitates.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of fine, coherent γ′-type ordered nanoprecipitates (e.g. Ni₃Ti or a related ordered phase with contributions from Al) uniformly dispersed within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening: the coherent γ′ nanoprecipitates effectively impede dislocation motion at elevated temperatures, thus enhancing yield strength and thermal stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-added alloy will exhibit an approximately 20–30% increase in yield strength at around 800°C compared to the baseline alloy lacking Al, with measurable precipitate volume fraction and coherence.
generation.baseline: The original Ti35Ni35Fe10Co10Cr10 alloy with a single-phase matrix exhibiting primarily solid-solution strengthening.
generation.boundary: All elemental concentrations remain within the HEA definition (5–35 at%). The heat treatment is effective up to roughly 800°C and for durations near 1 hour.
generation.uncertainty: Variations in the precipitate volume fraction and coherence due to inter-element interactions may influence the magnitude of strengthening. Robust microstructural characterization is required to ensure reproducibility.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two batches: the baseline Ti35Ni35Fe10Co10Cr10 alloy and the modified Ti35Ni35Fe10Co10Cr5Al5 alloy. Subject both to a homogenization heat treatment at ~800°C for 1 hour. Use TEM and XRD to evaluate the formation, distribution, and coherence of γ′ nanoprecipitates, and perform tensile/compression tests at 800°C.
measurements: Precipitate size, volume fraction, and coherence via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-modified alloy does not exhibit at least a 10% improvement in yield strength relative to the baseline or if coherent γ′ precipitates are not clearly detected, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The addition of elements with similar metallic atomic radii but different crystallographic structures (Al and Ti) to the Co-Ni-Fe alloy caused higher solution strengthening by the element with a different crystallographic structure than the solvent. The solid solution strengthening coming from addition of 5 at. pct Al to the Co-Ni-Fe alloy is negligible, while the addition of 5 at. pct of Ti significantly increases the solid solution strengthening. The precipitation hardening effect related to the presence of (CoNi)3Ti phase caused by the addition of 5 at. pct Ti is comparable with the total effect of the 5 at. pct Al and 5 at. pct Ti addition, which caused the precipitation of γ′ ((NiCo)3AlTi). Precipitation hardening is much greater in the investigated alloys than the solid solution hardening. We showed a successful way for effectively strengthening the FCC-HEA system (NiCoFe) using a small Ti addition. The microstructure obtained in the M3 alloy consists of precipitates with an L12 structure and structurally coherent with FCC matrix. We showed one of the ways of searching for new high-entropy alloys.

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) have drawn significant attention due to their unique design and superior mechanical properties. Comprising 5–35 at% of five or more elements with similar atomic radii, HEAs exhibit high configurational entropy, resulting in single-phase solid solutions rather than intermetallic compounds. Additive manufacturing (AM), particularly direct energy deposition (DED), is effective for producing HEAs due to its rapid cooling rates, which ensure uniform microstructures and minimize defects. These alloys typically form face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structures, contributing to their exceptional strength, hardness, and mechanical performance across various temperatures. However, FCC-structured HEAs often have low yield strengths, posing a challenge for structural applications. In this study, a Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA was manufactured using the DED method. This study proposes that the addition of aluminum and titanium creates a γ + γ′ phase structure within a multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix, enhancing the thermal stability and coarsening the resistance and strength. The γ′ phase with an ordered FCC structure significantly improves the mech

Figure 7a,b show the SEM images of the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA. The matrix phase of the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA appeared as the γ phase of the FCC structure, and the γ′ phase of the ordered FCC structure was confirmed to be widely distributed in the form of dot-like pores. In addition, no additional precipitated phases appeared on the SEM images, and it was confirmed that the grain size of the γ phase was coarse. For the component analysis of the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA and each phase, a component analysis of the entire area and each phase was conducted. Figure 7c,d show the results of the EDS analysis of the deposited Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA for the γ and γ′ phases, respectively. The analysis confirmed that the Ni-rich γ phase solid solution with Al and Ti was formed first, followed by the formation of the γ′ phase solid solution with a (Ni, Co)3(Ti, Al) composition. The composition of the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA was like that of the designed composition; however, there was a compositional difference of 1~2% for each element. Table 3 shows the chemical composition of the developed HEA for both the γ and γ′ phases.

papers.title: Manufacturing of Ni‐Co‐Fe‐Cr‐Al‐Ti High‐Entropy Alloy Using Directed Energy Deposition and Evaluation of Its Microstructure, Tensile Strength, and Mic
papers.system: Ni‐Co‐Fe‐Cr‐Al‐Ti HEA (with a FCC matrix and ordered γ′ precipitates)
papers.approach: Used additive manufacturing (DED) to form a multicomponent FCC solid‐solution that is modified by the addition of Al and Ti to induce the formation of ordered γ′ precipitates.
papers.findings: The alloy showed a two‐phase (γ + γ′) microstructure. An optimal Al + Ti content was necessary to avoid formation of detrimental intermetallics (e.g. Ni₂AlTi for high Al/Ti ratios) and to obtain the fine dispersion of γ′ precipitates, which provided good thermal stability and strength retention around 800 °C.
papers.mechanism: Precipitation hardening via coherent γ′ phase formation in an FCC matrix enhances yield strength at elevated temperatures.

papers.title: Remarkable Enhanced Mechanical Properties of TiAlCrNbV Medium-Entropy Alloy with Zr Additions.
papers.system: TiAlCrNbV medium‐entropy alloy with a small range of Zr additions
papers.approach: Systematic addition of varying amounts of zirconium with subsequent thermomechanical processing to tune grain size and solid‐solution strengthening.
papers.findings: As Zr content increased, yield strength increased by 3–8% and ductility trends improved; however, excessive Zr also led to grain coarsening. Thermomechanical treatment was needed to modify the microstructure to balance strength and ductility.
papers.mechanism: Solid solution strengthening from Zr (due to lattice distortion) coupled with grain size effects governs the mechanical response.

papers.title: The Effect of Al and Ti Additions on Solid Solution Strengthening and Precipitation Hardening in CoNiFe Medium-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: CoNiFe medium‐entropy alloy modified with small additions of Al and Ti
papers.approach: Investigated how adding 5 at.% Ti (and Al) affects strengthening through both solid solution and precipitation hardening, with a focus on the formation of (CoNi)₃Ti or γ′-like phases.
papers.findings: Addition of 5 at.% Ti significantly enhanced solid solution strengthening and induced the precipitation of an ordered phase (γ′ ((NiCo)₃AlTi)) that contributed more to total strengthening than the Al addition alone.
papers.mechanism: A combination of severe lattice distortion from Ti (solid solution strengthening) and precipitation hardening from coherent, ordered nanoprecipitates improves strength.

papers.title: Development of Precipitation-Strengthened Al₀.₈NbTiVM (M = Co, Ni) Light-Weight Refractory High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: Light-weight refractory HEA based on Al₀.₈NbTiV modified with minor Co or Ni additions
papers.approach: Designed alloys by incorporating Co or Ni (with smaller atomic radii) into a Ti-containing HEA to stimulate the formation of secondary sigma precipitates for improved high-temperature performance.
papers.findings: Addition of Co or Ni led to the formation of homogeneous sigma precipitates that enhanced room-temperature yield strength and provided superior specific yield strength (yield strength/density) at elevated temperatures compared to single-phase variants.
papers.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening via formation of sigma-phase particles—enabled by solid solution effects from small atomic size elements (Co/Ni)—reduces dislocation mobility at high temperatures.

papers.title: Manufacturing of Ti‐Nb‐Cr‐V‐Ni‐Al Refractory High‐Entropy Alloys Using Direct Energy Deposition.
papers.system: Ti‐Nb‐Cr‐V‐Ni‐Al RHEA, where Ti and Ni are among the principal constituents
papers.approach: Employed DED processing of mixed elemental powders to form a refractory alloy, analyzing phase formation (including sigma, BCC, and Ti₂Ni phases) and resulting fine-grained microstructures.
papers.findings: The alloy featured a complex microstructure with multiple phases; the rapid solidification during DED yielded a fine grain size that contributed to high hardness (~900 HV) and good elevated-temperature strength due to thermal shielding and refined microstructures in the heat-affected zone.
papers.mechanism: Combined effects of rapid solidification, fine grain strengthening, and dispersion of multiple phases help resist high-temperature deformation.

established: Precipitation strengthening (through ordered, coherent precipitates such as γ′ or sigma phases) can significantly enhance yield strength at elevated temperatures.
Solid solution strengthening via lattice distortion, especially by elements with large atomic radii differences, improves high-temperature mechanical properties.
Processing methods like DED and thermomechanical treatments can control grain size and phase distribution, further affecting high-temperature strength.

disagreements: The relative contributions of precipitate strengthening versus solid solution strengthening remain debated, with some papers emphasizing the critical role of coherent precipitates while others note the importance of grain size manipulation.
Some studies report that larger Zr additions can improve strength via lattice distortion, while others observe deleterious grain coarsening effects that counteract the intended strengthening.
open_questions: How does the deliberate primary incorporation of both titanium and nickel (as opposed to treating one merely as an addition) affect the balance of phase stability and precipitation behavior at elevated temperatures?
What is the optimal volume fraction, morphology, and coherent interface of precipitates in a Ti–Ni primary HEA to maximize yield strength without sacrificing ductility at high temperatures?

How do different processing techniques (e.g., DED versus conventional casting with thermomechanical treatment) impact the formation and stability of the desired microstructural features in Ti–Ni dominant systems?
opportunities: Designing a high-entropy alloy where titanium and nickel are the primary constituents and employing a controlled minor addition (e.g., a small amount of Al or Co) to induce a beneficial precipitation microstructure (γ′ or sigma) at elevated temperatures.
Combining rapid solidification techniques (such as DED) with post-deposition thermomechanical treatments to optimize grain size and precipitate dispersion in Ti–Ni primary HEAs.

Exploring non-equiatomic compositions that allow higher volume fractions of ductile, coherent precipitates while maintaining a high-entropy matrix, thereby extending the operating temperature regime with improved specific yield strength.

directions.direction: Composition design via minor alloying element additions to trigger precipitation strengthening.
directions.assessment: Adding a small amount of an element (e.g. Al) in a Ti–Ni primary HEA may induce coherent nanoprecipitates (γ′ or similar) that enhance elevated‐temperature yield strength. This approach directly targets the need for improved high‐temperature performance through precipitation strengthening and is supported by evidence in Ni-based systems (e.g., PMC11396108 and PMC10532893), though care must be taken with compositional boundaries.

directions.direction: Thermomechanical processing to refine grain size and control the precipitation distribution.
directions.assessment: Applying hot and cold rolling followed by rapid annealing can reduce grain size and improve precipitate dispersions. This grain refinement should lead to stronger grain-boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch) and enhanced precipitate effects. It is supported by studies on medium-entropy alloys (PMC9506522) but may require finely tuned processing to avoid adverse grain growth.

directions.direction: Targeted minor addition of a small atomic size element (e.g. Vanadium) to induce controlled sigma-phase precipitate formation.
directions.assessment: Introducing a low level (≈3 at.%) of vanadium may promote the formation of fine, dispersed sigma-phase precipitates that obstruct dislocation motion at high temperature. There is supporting evidence (PMC8074761 and PMC6170471) for sigma-phase strengthening, although controlling precipitate coarsening is critical.

directions.direction: Processing route using rapid solidification via Directed Energy Deposition (DED) to produce an ultrafine microstructure with homogeneously distributed nano-precipitates.
directions.assessment: Employing DED with a high laser energy density can yield rapid cooling, refining grain size and promoting a uniform nanoprecipitate distribution. The approach leverages direct evidence from DED-processed refractory HEAs (PMC9571103 and PMC11396108) and directly counters coarse microstructures from conventional casting.

directions.direction: Surface or coating interventions to protect and stabilize the microstructure at high temperature.
directions.assessment: While surface coatings may enhance oxidation resistance, they do not fundamentally modify the alloy’s bulk microstructure and strengthening mechanisms. This option is less direct in addressing the immediate target of yielding improved bulk elevated‐temperature mechanical properties.
